In the worst case, $O(N_{tri} \cdot N^3)$ if triangles span the entire grid, but typically much less due to bounding box culling [S1, S2].

The claim states that the worst-case complexity is $O(N_{tri} * N^3)$ if triangles span the entire grid, but typically less due to bounding box culling. Source [S1] describes an algorithm where each triangle iterates over a 3D grid of voxels (size $N^3$ where $N$ is resolution). The code explicitly calculates a bounding box for each triangle (`t_grid.min` to `t_grid.max`) and only iterates over voxels within that range. If a triangle spans the entire grid, the loop runs for all $N^3$ voxels for each of the $N_{tri}$ triangles, resulting in $O(N_{tri} * N^3)$. The bounding box calculation limits the iteration space for smaller triangles, supporting the 'typically much less' part of the claim. Source [S2] describes a different approach (SAT intersection per voxel) which is also $O(N_{voxels} * N_{tri})$ in the worst case, but [S1] provides the specific implementation details (bounding box culling) that align with the claim's reasoning.
